title: Shortest Uncommon Substring in an Array
statement:
You are given an array `arr` of `n` non-empty strings. Build and return an array `answer` of the same length `n`, where `answer[i]` is chosen like this:

- Look at the substrings (contiguous, non-empty pieces) of `arr[i]` that appear as a substring of no other element `arr[j]` with `j != i`.
- `answer[i]` is the shortest of them; when several have that shortest length, pick the lexicographically smallest one.
- If `arr[i]` has no such substring, `answer[i]` is the empty string `""`.
constraints: arr[i] contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

The strings are tiny (at most 20 characters, so at most 210 substrings each), which makes it affordable to list every substring of every string. The direct check, "does this piece appear inside any other string?", costs a scan of the whole array per piece. A hash map removes that scan: record, for each substring, how many different strings contain it. A substring of `arr[i]` with a count of exactly 1 can only belong to `arr[i]` itself, so it is uncommon.

## Approach

1. For each `word`, put all its substrings in a set `seen` (so a piece repeated inside one word counts once), then add 1 to `owners` for every piece in `seen`.
2. For each `word`, try lengths `1, 2, 3, ...` in order. Within one length, scan every start and keep the smallest `sub` whose count in `owners` is 1.
3. Stop growing the length as soon as `best` is found, since any longer piece loses. If no length works, `best` stays `""`.
4. Push `best` into `answer` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = ["cab", "ad", "bad", "c"]`. The counts include `a: 3`, `b: 2`, `c: 2`, `d: 2`, `ad: 2`, and `ca`, `ab`, `cab`, `ba`, `bad` with count 1. For `"cab"` no single letter works; at length 2, `"ca"` is found first and then the smaller `"ab"` replaces it, giving `"ab"`. Every piece of `"ad"` is shared, so it gets `""`. For `"bad"` length 2 yields `"ba"` (`"ad"` is shared). `"c"` also appears in `"cab"`, so it gets `""`. The result is `["ab", "", "ba", ""]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n·L³) with L ≤ 20: each of the n·L² substrings takes O(L) to slice and hash.
- Space: O(n·L³) for the map's keys in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- Count each substring once per string (use a set first); otherwise `"aa"` would count `"a"` twice and look shared with itself.
- Identical strings share every substring, so both get `""`.
- Shortest wins first; lexicographic order only breaks ties between pieces of the same length.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `owners` | substring → number of strings in `arr` that contain it |
| `seen` | distinct substrings of the current word |
| `start`, `end` | slice bounds of a substring |
| `length` | the substring length currently being tried |
| `sub` | the substring being examined |
| `best` | the chosen uncommon substring for the current word, or `""` |
| `answer` | the result array |
